parts.label: (a)
parts.text: State two different functions of capacitors in electrical circuits.

markscheme_points.text: Any valid two points e.g.: to store (electrical) energy; smoothing/reduce ripple (on direct voltages); to block d.c.; timing/time delay (circuits); in oscillator (circuits); in tuning (circuits); to prevent arcing/sparks

hints: Hint 1: Start by thinking about the basic property of a capacitor - it can hold separated charge on its plates and release it later. Where would that ability to store and release be useful?

Hint 2: Now think of a second, different behaviour - a capacitor blocks steady d.c. once charged but lets changing voltages through. Where is smoothing a varying voltage or creating a time delay useful?
parts.proper_answer: 1. To store electrical energy and release it when needed. 2. To smooth rectified d.c. / reduce ripple, or to block d.c. while allowing a.c. to pass.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **What a capacitor fundamentally does**
Think of a capacitor as a tiny rechargeable store. When connected to a supply it separates charge onto its two plates, storing energy as $E = \frac{1}{2}QV$. When disconnected it can then discharge and deliver that energy back to the circuit, for example in a camera flash or as a backup supply.

Step 2: **Other everyday circuit jobs**
Because $Q = CV$, a capacitor opposes changes in voltage. That makes it ideal for smoothing - filling in the dips in a rectified supply to reduce ripple. Once fully charged it also blocks steady d.c. but passes changing signals, so it is used for coupling, timing and time-delay circuits, oscillator and tuning circuits, and to prevent sparking across switch contacts.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text:
Three uncharged capacitors of capacitances $C_1$, $C_2$ and $C_3$ are connected in series with a battery of electromotive force (e.m.f.) $E$ and a switch, as shown in Fig. 6.1.

{{figure:figure_6_1}}

Fig. 6.1

When the switch is closed, there is a charge $+q$ on plate P of the capacitor of capacitance $C_1$.

Show that the combined capacitance $C$ of the three capacitors is given by the expression

$$\frac{1}{C} = \frac{1}{C_1} + \frac{1}{C_2} + \frac{1}{C_3}.$$

markscheme_points.text: clear indication of equal charge on each capacitor
$E = V_1 + V_2 + V_3$ and $V = Q / C$
completion of algebra leading to $1 / C = 1 / C_1 + 1 / C_2 + 1 / C_3$

hints: Hint 1: Look at Fig. 6.1 - the three capacitors form a single series loop with no branching. What does that tell you about the charge that ends up on each capacitor when plate P gets $+q$?
Hint 2: Think about voltages rather than capacitance directly. How is the battery e.m.f. $E$ shared between the three capacitors in series?
Hint 3: Write each voltage using $V = Q/C$ for the individual capacitors and for the single equivalent capacitor $C$, then divide through by the common charge to link $C$ to $C_1$, $C_2$ and $C_3$.
parts.proper_answer: Each capacitor carries the same charge $q$. $E = V_1+V_2+V_3$ with $V = q/C$, so $q/C = q/C_1+q/C_2+q/C_3$, giving $1/C = 1/C_1+1/C_2+1/C_3$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Why the charge is the same everywhere**
When the switch is closed, electrons flow from plate P round the loop. The $+q$ left on plate P attracts $-q$ onto the opposite plate of $C_1$. That isolated conductor between $C_1$ and $C_2$ must stay neutral overall, so $+q$ is pushed onto the next plate, and so on. The result is that each capacitor in series stores the same magnitude of charge $q$.

Step 2: **Add the voltages**
In a series loop the total driving voltage is shared. If the p.d.s across the three capacitors are $V_1$, $V_2$ and $V_3$, then by conservation of energy:
$$E = V_1 + V_2 + V_3$$

Step 3: **Use $Q = CV$ and complete the proof**
For each capacitor $V = Q/C$, so with common charge $q$:
$$V_1 = \frac{q}{C_1}, \quad V_2 = \frac{q}{C_2}, \quad V_3 = \frac{q}{C_3}$$
For the equivalent single capacitor $C$ that replaces the three, it would also hold charge $q$ with $E = q/C$. Substituting:
$$\frac{q}{C} = \frac{q}{C_1} + \frac{q}{C_2} + \frac{q}{C_3}$$
Dividing through by $q$ gives the required series result:
$$\frac{1}{C} = \frac{1}{C_1} + \frac{1}{C_2} + \frac{1}{C_3}$$

parts.label: (c)
parts.part_stem:
A student has available four capacitors, each of capacitance $20\mu\text{F}$.

Draw circuit diagrams, one in each case, to show how the student may connect some or all of the capacitors to produce a combined capacitance of:

parts.label: (c)(i)
hints: Hint 1: Recall that parallel adds capacitance ($C = C_1+C_2+...$) while series reduces it. To get $60\,\mu\text{F}$ from $20\,\mu\text{F}$ units you need a larger value, so which type of connection should you try and how many units will you need?
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Build up capacitance with parallel**
In parallel every capacitor sees the same voltage, so total stored charge adds. That means capacitances simply add: $C_{total} = C_1 + C_2 + ...$. Three $20\,\mu\text{F}$ capacitors side by side give:
$$C = 20 + 20 + 20 = 60\,\mu\text{F}$$
So draw three capacitor symbols with their top plates joined together and their bottom plates joined together.

enrichment.label: (c)(i)
hints: Hint 1: Recall that parallel adds capacitance ($C = C_1+C_2+...$) while series reduces it. To get $60\,\mu\text{F}$ from $20\,\mu\text{F}$ units you need a larger value, so which type of connection should you try and how many units will you need?

parts.label: (c)(ii)

markscheme_points.text: parallel combination of three capacitors connected

hints: Hint 1: You need $15\,\mu\text{F}$, which is smaller than $20\,\mu\text{F}$, so series must be involved. Try making a larger block first with parallel and then reducing it with one capacitor in series - what parallel block in series with $20\,\mu\text{F}$ gives $15\,\mu\text{F}$?
parts.proper_answer: Connect three $20\,\mu\text{F}$ capacitors in parallel to give $60\,\mu\text{F}$, then connect this combination in series with the fourth $20\,\mu\text{F}$ capacitor to give $15\,\mu\text{F}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Combine parallel then series**
First make a $60\,\mu\text{F}$ block as in (c)(i) using three capacitors in parallel. Then put that $60\,\mu\text{F}$ block in series with the remaining $20\,\mu\text{F}$ capacitor. For two capacitors in series:
$$\frac{1}{C} = \frac{1}{60} + \frac{1}{20} = \frac{1+3}{60} = \frac{4}{60}$$
$$C = \frac{60}{4} = 15\,\mu\text{F}$$
So the diagram shows three capacitors in parallel, with that whole group in series with the fourth capacitor.
